intro: Before you read a book closely, it helps to know how it is put together. This unit is about the shape of the Tanakh. You will learn its three parts and twenty-four books. You will learn the languages it is written in. You will meet the scribes and scholars who kept its text, and the handwritten scroll that is still read aloud every week. You will meet the Masoretes, who wrote down the vowels, and a scribe who counts every letter.

The second half of the unit is about reading. Jewish communities read the Tanakh in a yearly cycle, out loud and together. They fill its gaps with midrash. They speak of levels of meaning. And they print a verse in the middle of a page with commentators from many centuries arguing around it. In this tradition, to argue carefully about a text is to honor it.

By the end you will be able to name the three parts of the Tanakh. You will be able to explain how its order differs from the Christian Old Testament. You will be able to say what the Masoretes did and how a Torah scroll is made. You will know what a parashah and a haftarah are, and how peshat differs from derash. And you will be able to read a page of Rashi and say what question he is answering.
bigQuestion: How did the Tanakh get its shape and its text, and how does Jewish tradition read it?

timeline.t: Nehemiah 8 describes Ezra reading the Torah aloud to the people in Jerusalem
The Torah is translated into Greek in Egypt; the Septuagint begins
The Great Isaiah Scroll is copied; it will be found near the Dead Sea in 1947
Rome destroys the Temple; rabbis gather at Yavneh and discuss the last books of the canon
The Mishnah is edited; it already assumes the Torah reading and the haftarah
Genesis Rabbah and the Babylonian Talmud take shape, full of midrash
The Masoretes of Tiberias add vowels, accents and notes; the Aleppo Codex is written
The Leningrad Codex, the oldest complete Masoretic Bible, is finished in Cairo
Rashi lives in Troyes, France, and writes his commentary on the Tanakh and Talmud
Rashi's commentary becomes the first dated Hebrew printed book
Bomberg's Rabbinic Bible in Venice sets the Mikraot Gedolot page
Judith Kaplan marks the first bat mitzvah in the United States, in New York

words.d: the Hebrew Bible; the name is made from the first letters of Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim
the official list of books a community counts as its scripture
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible whose order shaped the Christian Old Testament
a language close to Hebrew used in parts of Daniel and Ezra and in the Targums
Jewish scholars of about the 7th to 10th centuries CE who added vowels, accents and notes to the Hebrew text
a handwritten book with pages; the Aleppo and Leningrad codices are the great Masoretic Bibles
a trained Jewish scribe who writes Torah scrolls by hand on parchment
the weekly Torah portion; there are 54 in the yearly cycle
the reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah portion
rabbinic searching of a text; a story or explanation that fills a gap or explains an oddity in a verse
the plain, contextual meaning of a verse, as opposed to derash, the searched-out meaning
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105) of France, author of the most studied Jewish commentary

test.q: Which of these correctly lists the three parts of the Tanakh?
choices: Torah, Talmud, Midrash
Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus
Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim
Law, History, Prophets
test.why: Tanakh is an acronym for Torah (Teaching), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).

test.q: Why does the Tanakh have 24 books while a Protestant Old Testament lists 39?
choices: The Tanakh leaves out the Prophets
The Old Testament includes the Talmud
The Tanakh counts only the Torah and the Writings
The Tanakh counts Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra-Nehemiah and the Twelve as one book each
test.why: The texts are the same; the Jewish count joins books that Christian Bibles split.

test.q: Which book closes the Tanakh, and with what?
choices: Chronicles, with Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem
Malachi, with a warning of judgment
Deuteronomy, with Moses's death
Esther, with the feast of Purim
test.why: The Tanakh ends with 2 Chronicles 36:23; the Christian Old Testament ends with Malachi.

test.q: What language are parts of Daniel and Ezra written in?
choices: Greek
Aramaic
Latin
Arabic
test.why: Daniel 2–7 and sections of Ezra are in Aramaic, a language close to Hebrew that many Jews spoke after the exile.

choices: Translated the Torah into Aramaic
Divided the Torah into 54 portions
Added vowel points, accents and margin notes to the consonant text
Wrote the book of Chronicles
test.why: Between about the 7th and 10th centuries CE, the Masoretes fixed the traditional reading with marks and notes, without changing the letters.

test.q: Why is the Aleppo Codex incomplete today?
choices: It was never finished by its scribe
The Masoretes removed the Torah section
It was cut up and sold as bookmarks in 1525
About a third of its pages were lost after the synagogue in Aleppo was attacked in 1947
test.why: The codex, c. 930 CE, lost many pages, including most of the Torah, around the 1947 attack; what remains is in the Israel Museum.

test.q: What did comparing the Great Isaiah Scroll with the Masoretic text show?
choices: The text stayed nearly the same over about a thousand years
Isaiah was written by the Masoretes
The scroll was a Greek translation
Half of Isaiah was missing from the Masoretic text
test.why: The Dead Sea Isaiah scroll of c. 125 BCE and the Masoretic Isaiah agree in nearly every word.

test.q: Which of these makes a Torah scroll pasul, unfit for use?
choices: Being written on parchment
A missing letter or two letters that touch
Having no vowel marks
Being more than fifty years old
test.why: Any error or damage makes the scroll unfit until repaired; scrolls are meant to have no vowels and are written on parchment.

choices: The last portion of Deuteronomy
A mystical level of meaning
A reading from the Prophets chanted after the Torah portion
The pointer used to follow the text
test.why: The haftarah comes from the Nevi'im and is matched to the Torah portion or the holiday.

test.q: On Simchat Torah, what do congregations do?
choices: Read the book of Esther with noisemakers
Bury worn-out scrolls
Fast and read Lamentations
Finish Deuteronomy and begin Genesis again, with dancing
test.why: Simchat Torah, rejoicing in the Torah, closes and restarts the yearly cycle in one day.

test.q: The story of young Abraham smashing idols comes from where?
choices: A midrash in Genesis Rabbah
Genesis chapter 12
The book of Daniel
Rashi's comment on Genesis 1:1
test.why: The Torah gives no reason for Abraham's call; Genesis Rabbah fills that gap with the idol story.

test.q: A reader asks what a verse means in its plain context. Which level is that?
choices: Derash
Peshat
Remez
Sod
test.why: Peshat is the plain sense; derash is searched-out meaning, remez is hint, and sod is secret.

test.q: What was Rashi's method as a commentator?
choices: Long essays on grammar with no midrash
Counting the letters of each book
Short verse-by-verse notes that raise a question and answer it with plain sense or a chosen midrash
Translating each verse into French
test.why: Rashi quotes a phrase, asks what problem it raises, and answers with peshat or with the midrash that fits the words.

test.q: What is printed in the center of a Mikraot Gedolot page?
choices: Rashi's commentary
The masorah notes
The haftarah for the week
The biblical verse, surrounded by Targum and commentaries
test.why: The verse sits in large type in the middle; Targum, Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban and others are printed around it.

test.q: In the Talmud's story of the oven, what verse does Rabbi Joshua cite and why?
choices: "It is not in heaven" (Deuteronomy 30:12), to say a heavenly voice cannot decide a debate among the sages
"Hear, O Israel" (Deuteronomy 6:4), to end the argument with prayer
"In the beginning" (Genesis 1:1), to prove Rabbi Eliezer right
"Let him go up" (2 Chronicles 36:23), to send the sages to Jerusalem
test.why: Rabbi Joshua's citation makes the point that interpretation is settled by the majority of the sages, not by miracles.

write.prompt: Does Jewish tradition treat the text of the Tanakh as fixed or as open? Argue your answer using at least two of these: the scribe's rules and the Masoretes' counting (chapter 15), the story of the oven with Deuteronomy 30:12 (Bava Metzia 59b), Rashi on Genesis 1:1, and the midrash on Abraham and the idols (Genesis Rabbah 38:13). Explain what each shows and how Jewish readers have understood it.
tips: Name each text you use: the book, chapter and verse, or the tractate and page, or the commentator and the verse he is explaining.
Attribute every belief: write "Jewish tradition holds" or "the rabbis taught," not "it is true that."
Use the unit's terms, such as masorah, peshat, derash and midrash, and explain each the first time.
It is fine to answer "both": show how the letters can be fixed while the meaning stays open.
Compare readers rather than judging them; say what question each one is asking.
